extracted.intended_audience: psychology researchers and practitioners studying humor temperament; questionnaire developers; applied humor researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Use the State-Trait-Cheerfulness-Inventory (STCI) framework to assess temperamental dimensions that determine how readily a person enters the comic frame and how that affects perceived funniness. The page summarizes three trait dimensions, their state analogues, two virtue-related humor styles, and diagnostic questions for applying the framework to judging jokes or audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Low threshold for amusement; frequent positive affect; pleasure in humorous interaction; habitual smiling and laughing; composure in adversity (cheerful coping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals high in trait cheerfulness are more readily amused and therefore will generally rate stimuli as funnier. When evaluating humor, consider that a high-cheerful audience will have a lower amusement threshold and greater responsiveness to humorous cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for goal-directed, important activities; sober reflective attitude; higher threshold for amusement; lowered intrinsic interest in playfulness. Not the opposite of cheerfulness — one can be both serious-trait and cheerful-trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seriousness raises the amusement threshold and reduces intrinsic interest in play; jokes that rely on playfulness or low-threshold cues may fail with high-seriousness individuals even if they are not in a negative mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait bad mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency toward sadness/ill humor; sullenness, irritability; reduced reward responsiveness; higher threshold for amusement, similar to seriousness but driven by negative affect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad mood reduces responsiveness to reward and humor, increasing the threshold for amusement. Distinguish failures of humor landing due to elevated threshold from those due to principled dislike (e.g., ethical objection).

rubrics_metrics.name: State analogues (state cheerfulness / state seriousness / state bad mood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each trait has a state form: a person can momentarily be more cheerful, serious, or in a bad mood than their trait baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor depends on the perceiver's state at the moment of perception, not trait alone. When predicting whether a joke will land, assess both trait dispositions and current state (e.g., someone low in trait cheerfulness might nonetheless be in a cheerful state and find something funny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience temperament determines perceived funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke does not have a fixed funniness rating — its funniness depends on the temperament/state of the perceiver. The same stimulus is funnier to high-cheerful audiences than to low-cheerful, to audiences in a cheerful state than a serious state, and to audiences not in bad mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of 'is this funny' must specify the audience temperament profile and state. When testing or reporting funniness, indicate the target audience's cheerfulness/seriousness/bad-mood profile and current state to make results interpretable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolent humor (virtue-related style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treats human weakness and wrongdoing benevolently — with sympathy and acceptance. Smile of understanding rather than ridicule. Aligns with virtues of kindness and forgiveness: 'We all err, and there is something endearing about it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a style, benevolent humor is evaluated by its compassionate stance toward targets; it is more likely to be acceptable to audiences valuing kindness and may succeed even with higher-seriousness listeners if it signals warmth rather than derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective humor (virtue-related style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims to correct and improve wrongdoing through humor. The bite of satire turned to ethical purpose. Aligns with the virtue of justice: 'By laughing at this fault, we may discourage it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective humor is evaluated by its perceived ethical aim and effectiveness in critiquing behavior. It may invite approval from audiences prioritizing justice but risks alienating those who see it as punitive or mean-spirited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework distinction from Martin's HSQ
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruch's framework focuses on (1) temperamental disposition to enter the humor frame and (2) virtue orientation (benevolent vs. corrective), whereas Martin's four-style framework emphasizes social functions (affiliative, aggressive, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose Ruch's framework when the goal is to account for individual differences in tendency to be amused and moral stance of humor; use HSQ when analyzing social-function roles of humor. The distinction affects which evaluative criteria you prioritize (temperamental thresholds and virtue posture vs. social function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic assessment questions for predicting humor reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to ask when evaluating whether humor will land: What is the audience's trait cheerfulness/seriousness/bad-mood profile? What is their current state along these dimensions? Does the humor adopt a benevolent posture toward human flaws or a corrective one? Does the joke require a low threshold of amusement (high-cheerful audience) or can it land even with a serious/bad-mood audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these diagnostic questions as a checklist before judging a joke's likely success or before reporting empirical funniness ratings. Explicitly specify both trait and state assessments and the humor's posture (benevolent vs corrective) to clarify applicability of any judgment.
